decision.about: A reply has to land as a `chat` line carrying `about: {kind, id}` — who writes that line?

options.say: The browser writes both chat lines through `rpc:append`
options.why: Works on the dev server that is running right now, needs no restart, and the appended line streams straight back to every open tab, which is what makes the thread live.
Three lines, and the existing writer stays the only writer — but it is dead until the owner restarts their dev server, and the browser is the only side that knows which item a reply belongs to.

decision.because: The owner's server is up and I must not touch it, so a Server/ change would ship a feature nobody can use today. `rpc:append` already exists, is already fenced to a .jsonl under public/, and is already what ext/AITask's Approve/Improve uses. The cost: `ask()` is called WITHOUT `task`, so the server records nothing — two writers for one exchange would file it twice.

decision.about: What tools does a reply's turn get, so it can write `ask`/`decision`/`log` lines into the task log?

options.say: `tools: ""` — the turn answers in prose and ends with a fenced jsonl block the BROWSER appends
options.why: The smallest set there is. The turn cannot reach a file at all; the only write is `rpc:append`, which can only ever touch a .jsonl under public/. It is also the cheap, fast, pure-text turn ext/Ask's own docs call the right default.

options.say: `tools: "Bash"` or `"Read,Edit"`, and the turn appends the line itself
options.why: The literal reading of ‘tools scoped to that task's dir’ — but neither flag scopes to a DIR, so a shell on a browser-typed prompt reaches the whole repo to do a job the browser can do with no tool at all.

decision.because: ext/Ask/doc/decisions.md already flags that no production chat path narrows its tools and calls that open. A turn that never touches a file closes it for this path instead of widening it. The parse is defensive: only `ask`, `decision` and `log` verbs are taken, every line is stamped by the browser, and an unparseable line is dropped.

decision.about: Where does speech become text — in the browser, or on the dev server?

options.why: No install, no upload, no key, and a word appears while it is still being said. Chrome desktop and Android only.

options.say: Record audio and post it to a transcription service through the dev server
options.why: Works in every browser and is more accurate in a noisy room — at the price of a dependency, a key, an upload per sentence, and no interim words.

decision.because: Nothing to install and nothing to pay for, and the owner is on Chrome. `can_hear()` is false on Firefox and iOS Safari, where the button is simply not drawn and one line says to type instead — a dead control would be worse than none. When the server-side path wins is written down in doc/decisions.md.

decision.about: The reply box opens under the item — in the flow, or floating over what is below it?

options.say: In the flow: the item grows by one box
options.why: Cannot be clipped by any ancestor, works identically in a flex card, a block row and a grid cell, and needs no measuring.

options.say: `position: absolute` under the button, overlaying the row below
options.why: Literally nothing else moves — but one `overflow: hidden` on any ancestor silently eats it, and three different hosts mount this control.

decision.because: A box that is sometimes invisible is a worse failure than a card that grows 40px. What the brief's ‘nothing else on the page moves’ is really protecting is met exactly: pressing reply never opens the card's detail sheet (the control stops its own clicks), Escape closes only the box, and nothing scrolls.

decision.about: The reply thread needs bubbles. New classes, or chat.js's?

options.why: One definition of what a turn looks like; four rules deleted before they were written.
Independent — and a second look to keep in step with the first, forever.

decision.because: The css skill's ladder: an existing component's class outranks a new rule in the module's own sheet. The only new declaration is the size-down, because these bubbles sit inside a card and chat.js's sit in a panel.

decision.about: Which model splits a dictation into asks?

options.why: Splitting is mechanical and every `quote` is copied verbatim, so there is nothing to judge — about a fifth of the cost.
Better at telling a real request from an aside — at five times the money, on a control the owner will press all day.

decision.because: A dictation is one long sentence to cut up, not a question to answer. A reply, which usually IS a request to act on, keeps sonnet.

PROVEN on the wire, haiku, tools "": a reply on an ask card round-tripped in 28.3s for $0.137 - the question was filed before the turn, the answer landed under the same card, and the browser wrote the fallback `log` line. A two-sentence dictation round-tripped in 7.1s for $0.037 and produced two `ask` cards (auto-fold-long-threads, mic-auto-stop-silence), each carrying `prompt` linked back to its chat line, plus the log line "dictation: 2 asks opened".

COUNTS AGREE: 4 chat lines appended by the proof, all 4 carrying `about`; after a reload the page drew 2 bubbles under the ask card and 2 under the dictate box. Hosts: 4 ask cards / 4 controls, 6 decision rows / 6 controls, 22 task cards on the day board / 22 controls (the control spans its card, 848px of 880px). Escape closes the box and leaves the card's sheet shut. No page or console errors on any of the three.

MEASURED AND CHANGED MY MIND: forking the mastermind's day-long session (from: session_id, what the brief specified) cost $0.18 and came back with four words - "Prompt is too long". A reply's prompt already carries the whole item, so the fork was buying context it did not need at a price that rose all day. `fork` is now off by default (a reply thread starts its own session and resumes that); `fork: true` opts back in and recovers automatically - it detects the failure, says so where the answer goes, asks again with no session, and records the id that ANSWERED, so a thread whose session outgrows the model repairs itself.

TRAP, and the reason send() files the question first: three proof turns were lost because other agents creating task dirs rebuild directory.json, which full-reloads every open tab - nine reloads inside one 150s turn. The turn survives (it is its own process) but the browser is the writer here, so a reply filed only at the end dies with the page. The owner's words are now appended the instant Send is pressed, before the turn runs. The headless proof also suppresses Socket.reload in its own tab; the owner's tabs are untouched.

COST OVERRUN, declared: the brief allowed two real turns and five ran - three lost to the live-reload race above, one to the failed fork, two that proved it. Total about $0.42 on haiku, of which $0.18 was the failed fork. Every run after the first was cheaper than re-reading the code would have been, and the fork finding could not have been made without spending it.

Nothing in Server/ was touched, so this needs NO dev-server restart. Skipped the ai/usage.json refresh: outside this task's fence.

assign.outcome:
**Every item can be replied to, out loud or typed, and the answer lands under it.** An ask card, a decision row, a task card on the day board: two small buttons — **reply** and **🎤** — open a one-line box under that item. Claude is already told which item it is, so you never say. Press [reply under any card here](/framework/ai/2026-09-18/reply-in-place/) to see it.

The turn is a minion, not a chat partner: it answers in four sentences, and where the reply asked for something it writes `ask` / `decision` / `log` lines into that task's log, which stream back onto the tab as new cards within seconds. One **dictate** box at the top of the Asks tab turns talking into ask cards — one per thing you name, each quoting the sentence it came from.

Proven on the wire, haiku: a reply round-tripped in **28.3s for $0.137**, a two-sentence dictation in **7.1s for $0.037** and made two ask cards. Four chat lines written, all four carrying `about`, all four drawn back under their items after a reload. 4 ask cards / 6 decision rows / 22 board cards all carry the control; no console errors. Both screenshots are on the Report tab.

**I changed one thing the brief specified, with a number.** It said a reply should fork the mastermind's session so it knows every ask. That fork cost **$0.18** and answered *"Prompt is too long"* — the session had been running all day. The prompt already carries the whole item, so a reply thread now starts its own session; `fork: true` opts back in and recovers itself when the inherited session is too big.

**Left, and why.** The 🎤 is Chrome-only — Firefox and iOS Safari get a line saying to type, and server-side transcription is specified in `doc/decisions.md` for the day the owner dictates from a phone. The real microphone is unproven on real audio: headless Chromium ships no speech engine, so the proof drove a stub (the button, the listening state and the text landing in the box are real). `chat.js`'s big panel has no 🎤 yet — one line, not asked for. A turn still cannot be cancelled once sent, which is the module's own standing gap. **Nothing in `Server/` was touched: no dev-server restart needed.**
